Bank Churn Prediction

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

Businesses like banks which provide service have to worry about problem of 'Customer Churn' i.e. customers leaving and joining another service provider. It is important to understand which aspects of the service influence a customer's decision in this regard. Management can concentrate efforts on improvement of service, keeping in mind these priorities.

Objective¶

You as a Data scientist with the bank need to build a neural network based classifier that can determine whether a customer will leave the bank or not in the next 6 months.

Data Dictionary¶

  • CustomerId: Unique ID which is assigned to each customer

  • Surname: Last name of the customer

  • CreditScore: It defines the credit history of the customer.

  • Geography: A customer’s location

  • Gender: It defines the Gender of the customer

  • Age: Age of the customer

  • Tenure: Number of years for which the customer has been with the bank

  • NumOfProducts: refers to the number of products that a customer has purchased through the bank.

  • Balance: Account balance

  • HasCrCard: It is a categorical variable which decides whether the customer has credit card or not.

  • EstimatedSalary: Estimated salary

  • isActiveMember: Is is a categorical variable which decides whether the customer is active member of the bank or not ( Active member in the sense, using bank products regularly, making transactions etc )

  • Exited : whether or not the customer left the bank within six month. It can take two values 0=No ( Customer did not leave the bank ) 1=Yes ( Customer left the bank )

# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram
In [188]:
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

# function to plot stacked bar chart


def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left",
        frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Write down the logic for choosing the metric that would be the best metric for this business scenario.

-

The model can make incorrect predictions in two ways:

Predicting that a customer is leaving when they are actually staying (False Positive). Predicting that a customer is staying when they are actually leaving (False Negative).

Which case is more critical?

The second case, predicting that a customer will stay but they are actually leaving (False Negative), is more concerning. This can lead to significant financial losses for the bank because, due to the misidentification, the bank may miss opportunities to engage with and retain these at-risk customers.

How can this loss be reduced (i.e., how to minimize False Negatives)?

To reduce False Negatives, the bank should prioritize improving Recall. A higher Recall reduces the likelihood of missing customers who are about to leave. Therefore, the focus should be on increasing Recall by accurately identifying True Positives (i.e., customers who are indeed planning to leave), which allows the bank to take proactive measures to retain them.

Function for plotting the confusion matrix

In [220]:
def make_confusion_matrix(actual_targets, predicted_targets):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    actual_targets: actual target (dependent) variable values
    predicted_targets: predicted target (dependent) variable values
    """
    cm = confusion_matrix(actual_targets, predicted_targets)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(cm.shape[0], cm.shape[1])

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

Neural Network with SGD Optimizer¶

In [222]:
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators ensures that we get the same output every time.
np.random.seed(2)
random.seed(2)
tf.random.set_seed(2)
In [223]:
#Initializing the neural network
model_0 = Sequential()
# Adding the input layer with 64 neurons and relu as activation function
model_0.add(Dense(64, activation='relu', input_dim = X_train.shape[1]))
#Adding 1st hidden layer with 32 neurons
model_0.add(Dense(32, activation='relu'))
# Let's add output layer and since the output of the prediction is either 1 or 0 , we will go ahead and use Sigmoid activation function in the output layer
model_0.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))
In [224]:
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(0.001)

# Let's use Recall as a metric in this case
metric = keras.metrics.Recall()
In [225]:
# Let's compile the model with SGD optimizer and binary cross entropy as loss with recall as metrics
model_0.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=optimizer,metrics=[metric])

Loss Function

In [228]:
#Plotting Train Loss vs Validation Loss
plt.plot(history_0.history['loss'])
plt.plot(history_0.history['val_loss'])
plt.title('model loss')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

The validation and training loss are both decreasing, but overfitting still seems to be occurring. The training data does not contain noise. However, the loss function occasionally fluctuates significantly during training, which slows down convergence. These fluctuations are likely due to noisy parameter updates. Let’s check other metrics to get a clearer understanding.

In [229]:
#Plotting Train recall vs Validation recall
plt.plot(history_0.history['recall'])
plt.plot(history_0.history['val_recall'])
plt.title('model recall')
plt.ylabel('Recall')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Confusion Matrix

In [235]:
make_confusion_matrix(y_train, y_train_pred)
In [236]:
make_confusion_matrix(y_val, y_val_pred)

The model performs well on class 0 (majority class) with high precision, recall, and F1-score. However, performance on class 1 (minority class) is poor, especially in terms of recall (only 17% of actual class 1 instances are identified in training set and only 14% of actual class 1 instances are identified in validation set), leading to a low F1-score. The model likely needs improvement in handling the minority class (class 1).

# Adding the output layer
model_1.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))

Loss Function

In [243]:
#Plotting Train Loss vs Validation Loss
plt.plot(history_1.history['loss'])
plt.plot(history_1.history['val_loss'])
plt.title('model loss')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

The model is overfitting, a common issue in deep learning due to the large number of parameters. Early stopping is an effective solution. During training, the model is evaluated on a validation set after each epoch. If performance on the validation set worsens or shows no improvement (e.g., increasing loss or decreasing accuracy), training is stopped. The model at this point is chosen for its better generalization.

This simple yet powerful method helps prevent overfitting.

plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Training Set: The model performs well with high precision, recall, and F1-scores for both classes, indicating good fit on the training data. Validation Set: The model's performance drops, particularly for Class 1, showing lower precision, recall, and F1-score. This suggests that while the model performs well on training data, it does not generalize as effectively to unseen validation data.

Neural Network with Adam Optimizer and Dropout¶

In [252]:
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(2)
random.seed(2)
tf.random.set_seed(2)
In [253]:
#Initializing the neural network
model_2 = Sequential()
#Adding the input layer with 32 neurons and relu as activation function
model_2.add(Dense(32,activation='relu',input_dim = X_train.shape[1]))
# Adding dropout with ratio of 0.2
model_2.add(Dropout(0.2))
# Adding the first hidden layer with 16 neurons with relu as activation functions
model_2.add(Dense(16,activation='relu'))
# Adding dropout with ratio of 0.1
model_2.add(Dropout(0.1))
# Adding the second hidden layer with 8 neurons with relu as activation functions
model_2.add(Dense(8,activation='relu'))
# Adding the output layer
model_2.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))
In [254]:
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(0.001)
metric = keras.metrics.Recall()
In [255]:
#Let's compile the model with binary cross entropy as loss function and recall as the metric.
model_2.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=optimizer,metrics=[metric])

# Summary of the model
model_2.summary()

Loss Function

In [258]:
#Plotting Train Loss vs Validation Loss
plt.plot(history_2.history['loss'])
plt.plot(history_2.history['val_loss'])
plt.title('model loss')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

From the plot, we observe that both the training and validation curves are smooth. This indicates that reducing the number of neurons and adding dropout layers effectively addressed the overfitting issue.

plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

#classification report
cr=classification_report(y_train,y_train_pred)
print(cr)

           1       0.84      0.49      0.62       998

    accuracy                           0.88      4900
   macro avg       0.86      0.73      0.77      4900
weighted avg       0.87      0.88      0.86      4900
In [264]:
#classification report
cr = classification_report(y_val,y_val_pred)
print(cr)

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.88      0.96      0.92      1672
           1       0.74      0.50      0.60       428

    accuracy                           0.86      2100
   macro avg       0.81      0.73      0.76      2100
weighted avg       0.85      0.86      0.85      2100

Training Set: The model performs well with high precision and recall for Class 0. However, for Class 1, the recall is lower, indicating that the model has difficulty identifying Class 1 instances.

Validation Set: Performance on the validation set is slightly lower but still strong, with a notable decrease in recall for Class 1 compared to training. This suggests some overfitting but overall good generalization.

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE) and SGD Optimizer¶

Let's apply SMOTE to balance the dataset and then perform hyperparameter tuning accordingly.

In [267]:
sm  = SMOTE(random_state=42)
X_train_smote, y_train_smote= sm.fit_resample(X_train,y_train)
print('After UpSampling, the shape of train_X: {}'.format(X_train_smote.shape))
print('After UpSampling, the shape of train_y: {} \n'.format(y_train_smote.shape))

#Initializing the model
model_3 = Sequential()
# Adding input layer of 32 neurons with relu as activation function
model_3.add(Dense(32,activation='relu',input_dim = X_train_smote.shape[1]))
#Adding hidden layer with 16 neurons with relu as activation function
model_3.add(Dense(16,activation='relu'))
#Adding hidden layer with 8 neurons with relu as activation function
model_3.add(Dense(8,activation='relu'))
# Adding the output layer
model_3.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))
In [270]:
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(0.001)

metric = keras.metrics.Recall()
In [271]:
# Let's compile the model with binary cross entropy as loss function and recall as the metric
model_3.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=optimizer,metrics=[metric])

Training Set: The model performs equally well for both classes with balanced precision, recall, and F1-scores. The overall accuracy is 73%.

Validation Set: The model shows strong precision for Class 0 but significantly weaker precision for Class 1. The recall for Class 1 is much better (72%) compared to its precision (39%), indicating that while many Class 1 instances are identified, they are often misclassified. Overall, the model’s performance on the validation set suggests that while it performs well for the majority class (Class 0), it struggles with the minority class (Class 1). You might consider further adjustments, such as additional hyperparameter tuning, class weighting, or different resampling techniques to improve the model's performance, especially for the minority class.

In [296]:
cr=classification_report(y_val,y_val_pred)
print(cr)

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0       0.92      0.77      0.84      1672
           1       0.45      0.74      0.56       428

    accuracy                           0.76      2100
   macro avg       0.69      0.76      0.70      2100
weighted avg       0.83      0.76      0.78      2100

Training Set: The model performs well with high precision, recall, and F1-scores for both classes, achieving an accuracy of 86%. This indicates good performance and balance on the training data.

Validation Set: Performance on the validation set shows a strong precision for Class 0 and a decent recall for Class 1. However, precision for Class 1 is quite low (0.45), while recall is higher (0.74). This suggests that while the model identifies many Class 1 instances, a significant number of them are misclassified as Class 0.

Overall, the model demonstrates strong performance on the training set but faces challenges with Class 1 precision on the validation set.

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE), Adam Optimizer, and Dropout¶

In [299]:
backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(2)
random.seed(2)
tf.random.set_seed(2)
In [300]:
#Initializing the model
model_5 = Sequential()
# Adding input layer of 32 neurons with relu as activation function
model_5.add(Dense(32,activation='relu',input_dim = X_train_smote.shape[1]))
# Adding the dropout
model_5.add(Dropout(0.2))
# Adding hidden layer with 16 neurons with relu as activation function
model_5.add(Dense(16,activation='relu'))
# Adding the dropout
model_5.add(Dropout(0.1))
# Adding hidden layer with 8 neurons with relu as activation function
model_5.add(Dense(8,activation='relu'))
# Adding the output layer
model_5.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))
In [301]:
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01)
metric = keras.metrics.Recall()
In [302]:
# Let's compile the model with binary cross entropy as loss function and recall as the metric
model_5.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=optimizer,metrics=[metric])

model_5.summary()

Training Set: The model shows good performance with balanced precision, recall, and F1-scores for both classes, and an overall accuracy of 85%. This indicates effective learning from the training data.

Validation Set: Performance is slightly lower compared to the training set. Class 0 maintains strong precision but lower recall (0.74), while Class 1 has a higher recall (0.75) but lower precision (0.43). This suggests the model is better at identifying Class 1 instances but often misclassifies them as Class 0.

Class 1: The recall is high (0.77), but precision is lower (0.44), leading to a lower F1-score of 0.56. Overall, the model has a good accuracy of 75% and balances performance reasonably well across classes, with particularly strong precision for Class 0 and decent recall for Class 1.

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

Age-Based Retention Strategies:

Insight: Older customers are churning more than younger ones.

Recommendation: Review and tailor retention strategies to address the specific needs and preferences of older customers. This could involve:

Customized Services: Offering personalized services or products that cater to the preferences of older customers.

Targeted Communication: Developing targeted communication strategies to engage and retain older customers.

Feedback Mechanisms: Implementing feedback mechanisms to understand and address the concerns of older customers.

Tenure-Based Retention Strategies:

Insight: Clients with very short or long tenures are more likely to churn compared to those with average tenure.

Recommendation:

Segmented Retention Programs: Design retention programs for customers at different tenure stages, such as special incentives or offers for those who have been with the bank for a short or long period.

Lifecycle Management: Monitor customer lifecycle stages and proactively engage with those nearing the end of their tenure or who have recently joined.

High-Balance Customers:

Insight: Significant bank balance holders are churning, which could impact available capital for lending.

Recommendation:

Exclusive Benefits: Offer exclusive benefits or premium services to high-balance customers to enhance their loyalty.

Personalized Outreach: Increase personal engagement with high-balance customers to address their specific needs and concerns.

Gender-Based Retention Strategies:

Insight: A higher proportion of female customers are churning.

Recommendation:

Gender-Specific Programs: Develop targeted retention strategies or programs that address the needs and preferences of female customers.

Customer Surveys: Conduct surveys to understand why female customers are churning and tailor interventions accordingly.

Credit Card Holders:

Insight: Majority of churned customers have credit cards, but this might be coincidental given the high proportion of credit card holders.

Recommendation:

Credit Card Usage Analysis: Analyze credit card usage patterns and satisfaction levels. Consider offering loyalty rewards or enhanced features to credit card holders.

Customer Segmentation: Segment credit card holders based on their usage and satisfaction to identify at-risk customers.

Inactive Members:

Insight: Inactive members have a higher churn rate, and the proportion of inactive members is high.

Recommendation:

Reactivation Programs: Implement reactivation programs to convert inactive members into active ones. This could include:

Special Offers: Offering special promotions or incentives to inactive members to encourage them to become active.

Engagement Campaigns: Running engagement campaigns to re-engage inactive customers, such as targeted emails or personalized offers.

Customer Experience Improvements: Enhance the overall customer experience to reduce inactivity and improve retention.

Conclusion

By addressing these specific areas—age, tenure, balance, gender, credit card use, and inactivity—the bank can develop targeted strategies to improve customer retention and reduce churn. Implementing these recommendations will help in tailoring services and interventions to meet the needs of various customer segments, ultimately leading to better customer satisfaction and loyalty.
